questions.q: According to the material, a definition explains the meaning, scope and ______ of a term.
Which of the following is NOT given as a reason why definitions matter?
options: They build common ground among diverse audiences

questions.q: "A sensor is a device that detects changes in physical conditions and converts them into measurable signals." Which word names the broader class to which a sensor belongs?
The slide compares using the wrong type of definition to "using a spoon to drive a nail." What does this comparison imply?
options: Any definition works if it is long enough
Only dictionary definitions are acceptable in research
Definitions should be avoided in research papers
The type of definition must be matched to the job, since purpose, audience and context decide it

questions.q: A student pastes a dictionary meaning into a research paper without thinking about the reader. Using the slide's statement that a dictionary definition ≠ a research definition ≠ an engineering specification, which criticism is most justified?
options: Dictionary definitions are always factually wrong
The definition may not serve the purpose and audience of a research paper
Research papers may not contain definitions
The definition should have been longer

questions.q: The slide lists "Essential foundation" as a reason definitions matter. For which kinds of text is this foundation described as critical?
Two engineers on one team use the word "node" differently and the design fails. Which listed benefit of definitions would have prevented this?
options: Building common ground and shared understanding among readers
Turning the term into a metaphor

questions.q: The Module 3 deck calls a definition "a precision tool" and says you need the right one for the job. Which conclusion follows?
options: One favourite definition type should be used everywhere
Only the shortest definition is precise
A definition should be judged by how well it fits its purpose, audience and context

questions.q: A writer gives a technical formal definition to an audience without technical backgrounds. Using the overview slide (choice depends on audience expertise, purpose and complexity), the best judgement is:
options: Wrong only because it is too short
A poor fit; an informal definition would suit that audience better
Ideal, because formal definitions are always best

questions.q: Which sentence best follows the pattern "term = class + distinguishing features" for the worksheet's "data logger"?
options: A data logger is like a notebook.
A data logger is an electronic instrument that records measurements of a physical variable automatically at set time intervals.
A data logger is useful in research.
A data logger is not a thermometer.

s1.label: 1.2 Formal, Informal, Operational and Negative Definitions (*Analysing Definitions* deck)

questions.q: A formal definition follows a three-part structure. What are the three parts?
For which readers is an informal definition described as ideal?
Which sentence is the INFORMAL definition of a diode, as given in the deck?
options: A diode is an electronic component that allows current to flow in one direction only.
A diode is basically a device that controls which way electricity can flow through it.
A diode is not a resistor because it passes current one way.
A diode is a component scoring above a set voltage in a test.

questions.q: "A tablet is not a desktop computer because it lacks permanent peripheral devices and relies on touch interfaces." What type of definition is this?
Why is a negative definition "rarely used alone"?
options: It tells readers what to exclude but not what to include
It cannot be written in technical fields

questions.q: "Intelligence is defined as a person's score on a standardised IQ test administered under controlled conditions." Which judgement is best supported by the deck?
options: It is negative because it says what intelligence is not
It is informal because it uses everyday words
It is operational because it specifies the test and conditions by which the concept is measured
It is formal because it names no procedure

questions.q: According to the overview slide, the choice of definition type depends on which three factors?
options: Audience's expertise, communication purpose and concept's complexity

questions.q: The recap gives: "A plot is saline when EC exceeds 4 dS/m." Which two things make this operational?
options: What is measured (EC) and the threshold (4 dS/m)
A word origin and a date

questions.q: The recap describes which type as "plain words, no three-part structure, for a non-technical reader"?
The deck says a negative definition "usually works best when combined with positive definition elements." Why?
options: It narrows scope by saying what something is not, but positive elements supply what it is
Negative definitions are illegal in research

questions.q: A lab needs a definition for quality control and standardisation, where measurable criteria matter. Which type does the deck's "when to use" guidance favour?
The recap defines an Extended definition as a formal definition developed with two to four methods of expansion. Which plan matches this?
options: Eight methods and no formal definition
A formal definition followed by two to four named expansion methods

s2.label: 1.3 Expanded Definitions: The Key Focus and Methods of Expanding Definitions

questions.q: Which list gives the eight methods of expansion in the *Analysing Definitions* deck?
options: Function, Structure, Process, Analogy, Example, History, Comparison, Etymology
Function, Structure, Negation, Analogy, Example, Cause, Comparison, Etymology
Formal, Informal, Operational, Negative, Extended, Lexical, Stipulative, Ostensive
Function, Structure, Process, Analogy, Visual Aids, History, Classification, Etymology

questions.q: Which situation does NOT call for an extended definition, according to the deck?
options: A concept with multiple components or processes
Academic reports needing supporting evidence and examples
A term that can be fully explained in one sentence to familiar readers

questions.q: "AI systems can learn from experience, recognise complex patterns in data, make informed decisions and adapt to new situations." Which method of expansion is this?
Why does the deck say strong extended definitions combine 2–4 methods?
options: Each method shows the concept from a different angle, layering comprehension
Four methods are required by every journal
One method alone is never allowed
More methods always shorten the definition

questions.q: A writer packs all eight methods into one paragraph. Judged against the deck's best practice, this is most likely to:
options: Be ideal, since more methods are always better
Break the rule that definitions must be one sentence
Overload the reader instead of strategically combining 2–4 methods while keeping engagement
Turn the definition into a negative definition

questions.q: How long do extended definitions typically run?
How does the deck describe an extended definition?
options: A comprehensive explanation using multiple methods rather than a single sentence

questions.q: Which situation is "When Audience Needs Context"?
options: The term has a single meaning
Readers lack specialised knowledge or need background to grasp significance
The report is for a journal

questions.q: A concept involves several components, processes and applications that cannot be explained in one sentence. Which heading from the slide fits?
How does By Analogy differ from By Comparison in the deck?
options: Analogy gives word origin; Comparison gives history
Analogy likens the term to familiar concepts; Comparison sets out similarities and differences
Analogy lists components; Comparison lists examples

questions.q: A writer repeats By Example four times and uses no other method. Judged against "varied explanatory techniques", this is:
options: Weaker, because layering different methods gives different angles

s3.label: 1.4 Extended Definition Breakdown: Artificial Intelligence (Parts 1 and 2)

questions.q: How does the deck's simple definition describe AI?
options: A branch of computer science concerned with creating machines that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence
A programme that follows fixed instructions only
A device that converts signals into measurements
A study of the human brain

questions.q: "The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined at the Dartmouth Conference in 1956." Which method of expansion is this?
"Artificial, from Latin *artificialis* meaning 'made by human skill'…" Which method is used?
Compare the By Function and By Process paragraphs. What is the key difference?
options: Function describes what AI enables it to do; Process describes a workflow from data input to improving outputs
Function lists AI's components; Process lists its inventors
Function gives its origin; Process gives its word roots

questions.q: A student labels "AI functions similarly to the human brain in its ability to learn from experience" as By Comparison. Which judgement is best?
options: Correct, because any likeness is comparison
Incorrect; it belongs to By Analogy, likening AI to a familiar concept

questions.q: Which pioneer does By History name as posing fundamental questions about machine intelligence in the 1950s?
"Algorithms that define decision-making rules, large datasets, neural networks, and hardware including processors and memory." Which method?
Which reasons does By History give for dramatic progress in the 21st century?
options: Fewer computers, small data, simple algorithms
Increased computational power, big data availability and algorithmic breakthroughs

questions.q: Which sequence matches the By Process workflow?
options: Data input, pattern analysis, learning algorithms adjust parameters, decisions or outputs improve over time
Pattern analysis, output, data input, learning
Learning, data input, output, pattern analysis
Output, data input, learning, pattern analysis

questions.q: The By Comparison paragraph contrasts AI with traditional programmes. Which claim does it best support?
options: AI needs a rule for every scenario
AI and traditional software are identical
AI adapts and learns from new data without explicit reprogramming, unlike fixed-rule software

questions.q: Which is the FIRST tip listed under "How to Score Well"?
options: Use as many bullet points as possible
Begin with a clear formal definition providing term, class and distinguishing features

questions.q: Which is a typical exam task listed in the deck?
options: Draw a flowchart of a research article
Convert a simple definition into an expanded, comprehensive one
Convert an APA reference into MLA

questions.q: The tips warn against "circular logic". Which sentence from the material is circular?
options: "A database is a base of data."
"A computer is a device used for gaming."

questions.q: The deck suggests "smooth transitions between expansion methods." What does this add to an extended definition?
options: Logical flow, so the methods read as one explanation

questions.q: You must write an extended definition of "blockchain" (one of the deck's practice terms). Which plan best follows the tips?
options: Open with a metaphor, then list synonyms
Use only one method to keep it short
Open with a formal definition, add three different expansion methods, and link them with transitions

questions.q: Tip 02 says to incorporate multiple expansion methods. How many techniques does it suggest aiming for?
A question asks you to "identify and label methods of expansion in a provided definition." Which typical exam task is this?
options: Identifying and labelling methods in a given definition

questions.q: Tip 03 warns against vague expressions and circular logic. Which pair of sentences best illustrates the two?
options: "A virus is something harmful" (vague) and "A database is a base of data" (circular)
"Love is a battlefield" (circular) and "A computer is a device used for gaming" (vague)
"A tablet is not a desktop" (circular) and "AI mimics intelligence" (vague)

questions.q: A student uses three methods but jumps between them with no links. Which tip is violated?
options: Ensure logical flow and smooth transitions between methods

questions.q: For the practice term "renewable energy", which plan best follows the tips?
options: Open with a formal definition, then use three or four different methods in a logical order

s5.label: 1.6 The 8 Types of Definitions, and Lexical vs Stipulative (*Module 3* deck)

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the 8 types on the slide?
"For this study, 'elderly' refers to individuals aged 60 and above." What type is this?
"Algorithm: a process or set of rules to be followed in calculations" — Oxford English Dictionary. What type is this?
An ostensive definition defines a term by:
options: Using a word with similar meaning

questions.q: Which statement about lexical and stipulative definitions is correct?
options: Lexical can be right or wrong and changes as language evolves; stipulative is neither right nor wrong, only agreed upon
Both can be right or wrong
Stipulative definitions describe what the world already agrees on
Lexical definitions are coined just for one paper

questions.q: A reviewer says a paper's stipulative definition of "elderly" (60 and above) is "wrong because the dictionary differs." Which response is best?
options: Agree; stipulative definitions must match the dictionary
Agree; the paper should be rejected
Disagree; the paper must use extensional listing
Disagree; a stipulative definition creates its own little world for the study and is just agreed upon

questions.q: Which type is "the theoretical essence of a concept within a field of study"?
"For this paper, 'node' means any connected device." Which type?
Which type defines by listing examples that belong to the term?
How does By Synonym differ from Extensional?
options: Synonym clarifies with a word of similar meaning; Extensional lists examples

questions.q: A study needs "elderly" to mean a fixed age range for this paper only. Which type is the best choice, and why?
options: Stipulative; it sets an agreed meaning for the study

questions.q: Genus & Difference is "broader category + what makes it unique within that category". Which sentence follows it?
options: "A diode is an electronic component that allows current to flow in one direction only."

questions.q: What does an operational definition specify?
options: How a concept is measured or observed

questions.q: Which is the OPERATIONAL version, rather than the vague one?
options: "Stress was measured using the PSS-10 scale; scores above 20 indicate high stress."
"Stress is the state of being stressed."

questions.q: Why do operational definitions make research "testable, repeatable"?
options: They name the measurement or procedure so others can repeat it

questions.q: "A tree is a perennial plant with a single woody stem, branches, and leaves…" The slide notes it doesn't say all trees must have leaves. What does that show about a descriptive definition?
options: It prescribes how trees should be
It describes what is commonly observed, without prescriptions or judgements

questions.q: Which rewrite best turns "Students who are stressed performed poorly" into an operational statement?
options: "Stress was measured with a named scale and a stated score threshold defined high stress."

questions.q: The heading says: "If You Can't Measure It, You Can't ______ It."
Which is listed under "When to use" an operational definition?
options: Research contexts, quality control, standardisation and measurable criteria

questions.q: Which is the DESCRIPTIVE definition?
options: "For this study, elderly means 60 and above."
"A tree is a perennial plant with a single woody stem, branches, and leaves, growing to a considerable height."
"Stress was measured using the PSS-10 scale."

questions.q: The descriptive definition says "how something is — not how it should be." What does this rule out?
For which concept type is a descriptive definition "especially powerful"?
options: Naturally occurring, complex or context-dependent concepts

s7.label: 1.8 Simple vs Extended Definitions, and Methods for Expanding a Definition (*Module 3* deck)

questions.q: The formula for a simple definition in this deck is:
Which sentence is the deck's simple definition of a smartphone?
options: A smartphone is a mobile device that combines phone and computer functions.
A smartphone is not a landline.
A smartphone is scored on a test.

questions.q: Which method appears in this deck's list of expansion methods?
"A firewall is like a security guard for your network — it checks IDs at the door." Which method is this?
"'Cyber' from Greek *kybernetes* = 'steersman.'" Which method is this?
How do Cause & Effect and Principles of Operation differ in the slide?
options: Cause & Effect asks how it works; Principles asks where it fits
Cause & Effect asks what produces it and what it produces; Principles asks how it actually works
Both ask where it fits in the larger system

questions.q: The deck says "when in doubt, extend." For a concept that is central, complex or contested, this advice is:
options: Sound, because such concepts need more than a simple definition
Unsound, because simple definitions are always better
Sound only for readers who already know the term

questions.q: According to the slide, an extended definition consists of:
options: A simple definition plus history, examples, types, functions and analogies

questions.q: "Renewable energy includes solar, wind, and tidal power." Which method?
"Machine learning is NOT just programming rules — it learns from data." Which method?
Which question does the Classification method ask?
options: Where does the word come from?
Where does it fit in the larger system?

questions.q: The slide says Visual Aids are used "because sometimes words just give up." Which situation best justifies one?
options: A concept whose structure is hard to convey in words alone

questions.q: Which set uses exactly three methods from this deck's list?
options: By History, By Structure, By Process

s8.label: 1.9 Definition Pitfalls: A Hall of Shame

questions.q: Which four pitfalls does the slide name?
options: Circular, too broad, too narrow, figurative only

questions.q: "A virus is something harmful" — so is bad Wi-Fi. What is the fault?
"A computer is a device used for gaming." What is the fault?
Worksheet item: "Heat stress is the body waving a white flag." Which fault fits and why?
options: Too broad, because it covers everything
Figurative, because it uses a metaphor instead of a precise meaning
Too narrow, because it names only one body

questions.q: Worksheet item: "Reflectance is the property of being reflective." Which is the most accurate evaluation and fix?
options: Circular; restate as how much light a surface throws back

questions.q: Why is "Love is a battlefield" "poetic, but useless in a research paper"?
options: It is figurative only and gives no precise meaning

questions.q: Worksheet: "A control group is the group that is not the experimental group." What weakness does it show?
options: It defines the term by negating a related term without saying what the group is

questions.q: "A database is a base of data" is described as "congratulations, you've said nothing twice." What does this mean?
options: The definition repeats the term instead of explaining it

questions.q: "A data logger is a device that is useful in research." Which rewrite best fixes the fault?
options: "A data logger is what a logger logs."
"A data logger is a helpful gadget."
"A data logger is an electronic instrument that records measurements of a physical variable automatically at set time intervals."

questions.q: Using the worksheet glossary ("the group that does not receive the treatment, used for comparison"), which is the best rewrite of the control-group definition?
options: A control group is the group that does not receive the treatment and is used for comparison.
A control group is the other group.
A control group is not experimental.
A control group is like a referee.

s9.label: 2.1 Surface Reading vs Deep Reading
s9.topic: Part 2: Reading Comprehension and Drawing Inferences

questions.q: Deep reading means understanding what the text:
options: Implies, assumes, and carefully avoids saying

questions.q: A paper says "Sample size: n = 12." Which is the DEEP reading?
options: The sample is small, so findings may not generalise beyond it.

questions.q: For the sentence "Average waste fell from 78 grams per plate in the first six weeks to 54 grams in the second six" (model paper), which is a sound DEEP reading?
options: Waste per plate was lower in the second half, but the sentence alone does not show what caused the fall

questions.q: The deck says "the gaps between the lines are often more revealing than the lines themselves." Why?
options: Because scientific texts are usually blank
Because what a text avoids saying or assumes shows its limits and confidence

questions.q: A student summarises a paragraph accurately and stops. Per the deck, this earns:
options: A gold star for surface reading, but not deep reading

questions.q: Using the reference box, "Stated" means the claim is:
options: Written on the page, so you could underline it

questions.q: Passage B says students with more than ninety minutes of pre-sleep phone use "scored significantly worse." Which is the best DEEP reading?
options: Phone use and poor sleep go together in the data, but the passage says direction cannot be established

questions.q: "The researchers chose the pre-monsoon season on purpose." The passage never says this. Which label fits a claim you brought with you?
How do Inferred and Speculated differ in the reference box?
options: Inferred: the passage makes it necessary and you can point to the forcing words; Speculated: it fits but nothing supports it
Inferred is written on the page
Inferred: nothing supports it; Speculated: forced by words

questions.q: The recap says deep reading is about "size, scope or reliability." A student notes only that "12 participants were studied." Judge.
options: Surface reading only; the small sample's implication for generalising is missing

s10.label: 2.2 How to Draw Inferences Like a Pro
s10.topic: Part 2: Reading Comprehension and Drawing Inferences

questions.q: Which is a hedging phrase given in the deck?
What does hedging tell the reader?
options: The authors are not sure and are being politely honest

questions.q: According to the deck, an inference is:
options: A reasoned conclusion drawn from evidence

questions.q: Passage A says night-time differences "were not statistically significant." Which inference is forced by these words?
options: The coating fails in the afternoon
The benefit is mainly a daytime one

questions.q: Why does the deck call the Limitations section "the most honest part of any paper"?
options: It is where authors state what they could not control or establish

questions.q: The recap says: "Always quote the words in the passage that ______ your answer."
Passage A says fan use "was self-reported and was not metered." Which evidence is weaker on fan use?
options: Residents' reports, since measured evidence beats self-reported belief

questions.q: "Challenge the data: does the graph actually support the claim in the text?" Which reader behaviour follows?
options: Comparing the claim with what the figure shows

questions.q: A reader says a passage "obviously" implies something but cannot point to any words that force it. By the worksheet's four labels, this reading is:
options: More likely assumed or speculated than inferred

questions.q: Which answer follows the worksheet's worked-example model (name the point, then quote the forcing words)?
options: "The benefit is mainly a daytime one; night-time differences were 'not statistically significant'."

s11.label: 2.3 Common Traps When Reading Research
s11.topic: Part 2: Reading Comprehension and Drawing Inferences

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four traps on the slide?
In the deck's ice-cream example, why does ice cream not cause drowning?
options: Both rise in summer, so they go together without one causing the other

questions.q: A reader says "self-service caused the fall in waste" (canteen passage). Which trap is this, and what makes it unsafe?
options: Jargon overload; the passage uses hard terms
Correlation read as cause; posters and a price rise also occurred and were not allowed for
Cherry-picking; only breakfast data were used
Overgeneralisation; the study covered ten canteens

questions.q: "This study proves…" is flagged as which trap, and why?
options: Overgeneralisation; one study suggests or indicates but proves nothing
Cherry-picking; it uses a small sample

questions.q: How does the deck advise you to handle dense terminology that may hide a weak argument?
options: Be curious and ask what it is actually saying

questions.q: Why does the deck say jargon can be a trap?
options: Dense terminology can disguise weak arguments

questions.q: Passage B says poor sleepers "may use their phones more because they are already awake." Which trap does this warn about?
options: Correlation being read as cause (the direction may be reversed)

questions.q: What does cherry-picking look like, and how does the deck say to guard against it?
options: Using long words; read the title
Highlighting only results supporting the hypothesis; read the full results section

questions.q: The canteen study is one canteen over one term, yet a reader recommends it for the whole institution. Which trap, per the recap?
Rewrite "This study proves self-service reduces waste" in line with the deck.
options: "This study suggests self-service may reduce plate waste."

s12.label: 3.1 IMRaD: The Universal Language of Science

questions.q: What does IMRaD stand for?
Which IMRaD section asks "Could someone else repeat it?"
"Mean daytime reduction was 2.1 °C (SD 0.6)." Which IMRaD section is this from?
Why does the deck say Results give "just the facts" while Discussion asks "What does it mean?"
options: Results report what the data showed; Discussion interprets, gives implications and what's next

questions.q: The deck says with IMRaD you can navigate research "even if you understand none of the actual science." Judge this claim.
options: Reasonable, because IMRaD is used in virtually every scientific journal, so the structure shows where to find each kind of content
Wrong, because each journal uses a different structure
Wrong, because science cannot be navigated

questions.q: Which question belongs to the Introduction?
options: What's the problem, and why should anyone care?

questions.q: A section reports tables and statistics with no interpretation. Which IMRaD section?
Why is Discussion placed after Results?
options: Meaning and implications can only be drawn from data already shown

questions.q: A Results section says "this proves the coating works." Against the deck ("just the facts"), the best judgement is:
options: It interprets and overclaims, which belongs (carefully) in Discussion

questions.q: Which sequence orders the four IMRaD parts correctly?

s13.label: 3.2 Anatomy of a Research Article: The Full Map (Parts 1 and 2), with the Recap's Section Table

questions.q: The recap says Literature review extracts carry which giveaway?
Which section's job is "what the data showed — numbers, no interpretation"?
The recap says the Conclusion does what?
options: Answers the opening question and says what remains to be tested

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches section to giveaway words?
The deck says "No references = no trust." Why?
options: They are the credibility receipt showing where claims came from

questions.q: How does the deck describe the Literature Review's message?
options: "Here's what everyone else has done — and here's the gap they all missed."

questions.q: What are the three moves of an introduction, in order?
options: Establish the Niche, Establish the Territory, Occupy the Niche
Establish the Territory, Establish the Niche, Occupy the Niche
Occupy the Niche, Establish the Territory, Establish the Niche
State results, State methods, State limits

questions.q: Why is Establish the Territory usually the most heavily cited paragraph?
options: It claims common ground with accepted knowledge

questions.q: Which words signal the "turn" in Establish the Niche?

"Although several studies have examined coating reflectance in temperate climates, none has assessed performance under sustained pre-monsoon dust loading." Which move does the pivot "none has assessed" perform?
The deck says "Find the hinge sentence and you have found the paper's reason for existing." Why?
options: Everything before is setup and everything after is delivery
It is always the last sentence of the paper

questions.q: What does the third move, Occupy the Niche, typically include?
options: The objective, sometimes the method, occasionally the finding, and often a map of the sections that follow

questions.q: A sentence says the field matters and states accepted knowledge in it. Which move?
Why is the hinge sentence placed between Move 1 and Move 3?
options: It turns from accepted knowledge to what is missing, which motivates the paper

questions.q: Draft: "Earlier work on hospital noise concentrated on intensive care units. General wards have been studied far less. This study measures night-time noise in four general wards." Judged by the three moves, this draft:
options: Establishes the territory, the niche, then occupies the niche

questions.q: Which sentence best supplies the missing "niche" turn between "Earlier work concentrated on ICUs" and "This study measures general wards"?
options: "However, general wards have been studied far less."

questions.q: What are the four questions of the abstract test?
Which vague phrase is called "a way of not reporting" a finding?
An abstract names no method, sample or period. Which question has no answer, and what does the deck call this?
options: How; the strongest early warning signal

questions.q: An abstract with no motive "usually fronts a paper with no argument". Which question is unanswered?
Which ordering correctly structures a seventy-word abstract for the model paper's noise study?
options: Method, findings, topic, why it mattered
What was studied, why it mattered, how it was done, what was found and what follows
Why it mattered, recommendations, method, topic

questions.q: What does the "What?" question test?
options: Whether the object of study can be named from the abstract

questions.q: An abstract says only "Results are discussed." Which question is unanswered?
"If one has no answer, you have learned something about the paper before reading it." What is learned?
options: The paper may be weak in that respect

questions.q: The model paper limits the abstract to seventy words and marks coverage, order and length. A draft covers all four questions in order but runs to 95 words. Judge.
options: Loses credit for exceeding the word limit despite good coverage and order

questions.q: For the noise study, which sentence best answers "Why did it matter?"
options: General wards have been studied far less than intensive care units.

s16.label: 3.5 Read in This Order, Not That One

questions.q: Which is the first item in the recommended reading order?
After the abstract, which item does the deck say to read next?
Why read Figures and Tables early?
options: They are the evidence itself, before anyone tells you what it means

questions.q: Why does the deck say skipping Methods is a problem?
options: Without knowing how the evidence was produced you cannot judge anything else

questions.q: A student reads front to back and gives up on page two. The deck's diagnosis is most likely:
options: Papers are printed in the order they are argued, not the order they are best read

questions.q: What does the Conclusion do when read second?
options: Tells you where the argument ends so you can watch it get there

questions.q: You want to know who a paper builds on and how recent it is. Which item?
Why do Introduction and Discussion come after Figures and Methods?
options: They are the argument wrapped around evidence you have now seen

questions.q: You have twenty minutes for a paper. Which first step does the deck support?
options: Read the abstract to decide if the paper is worth the next twenty minutes
Read every page in print order

questions.q: Which sequence lists the reading order correctly?
options: Figures, Abstract, References, Intro, Conclusion, Methods
References, Methods, Abstract, Conclusion, Figures, Intro
Abstract, Conclusion, Figures and Tables, Methods, Introduction and Discussion, References

questions.q: How many questions are in the Critical Reading Checklist?
"Each one can stop you." What does this mean?
options: You must answer all six in any order
If an early answer is no, later questions matter much less

questions.q: A paper's conclusions hold for a population the study never sampled. Which checklist question does it fail?
options: Does the discussion follow from the results?
Are the results presented without spin?

questions.q: Which is given as a "poor answer" to "Are the results presented without spin?"
options: An aim so broad no result could contradict it
Axes that start above zero; significance claimed without a test
One sentence conceding only the obvious

questions.q: "Confidence is not evidence. A well-dressed argument is still only an argument." Which reader response follows this?
options: Look for the data that support the claim

questions.q: Which is the first checklist question?
options: Is the research question stated, and specific?

questions.q: An aim is "so broad that no result could contradict it." Which question fails?
options: Is the research question stated, and specific?

questions.q: A method "measures something adjacent to what was asked." Which question fails?
options: Is the method appropriate to that question?

questions.q: Why are limitations described as poorly acknowledged if there is "one sentence at the end conceding only what is obvious"?
options: It gives the reader little real sense of what could not be concluded

questions.q: A confident paper lacks supporting data for its main claim. Which checklist question does it fail, and why?
options: Is every claim supported? Assertion with confidence is not evidence

questions.q: Which ordering of questions matches the checklist?
options: Claims, limitations, method, question, discussion, results
Question, method, results, discussion, limitations, claims
Limitations, question, results, method, claims, discussion
Results, question, claims, method, discussion, limitations

questions.q: IMRaD is the convention of which type of scholarship?
